title: OpenAI backs a shared robots.txt signal for AI training preferences
dek: An October 30 Internet-Draft defines a cross-provider policy token that reuses existing robots.txt syntax but keeps training preferences separate from crawler access.
evidence: OpenAI October 30 commitment and the original October 30 individual IETF Internet-Draft; proposed syntax is documented, but provider support is not yet deployed
takeaway: Permission to crawl and permission to train are distinct decisions. A shared robots.txt policy token can express both without changing existing crawler behavior.

sections.title: Context

bullets.detail: Website operators commonly express restrictions through crawler-specific User-agent groups. Those rules do not by themselves provide a common, purpose-specific signal about training generative models.

paragraphs: Per-crawler controls: Website operators commonly express restrictions through crawler-specific User-agent groups. Those rules do not by themselves provide a common, purpose-specific signal about training generative models.

sections.title: What's new

bullets.detail: The draft defines User-agent: __usage_ai-training. Standard Allow and Disallow path rules express preferences about using retrieved content to modify generative-model parameters; no new robots.txt directive is introduced.
The training policy group does not govern whether a bot may fetch a page. Crawler-specific rules still control crawling. A wildcard User-agent: * group does not count as an AI-training preference.

A site can express a preference against training on most paths while allowing it for selected paths. If no matching policy-token group exists, the draft treats the training preference as unspecified, not as explicit consent.
OpenAI says it will honor the shared signal alongside existing crawler-specific controls. Implementation is planned for the coming months, not announced as already active.

sections.title: Evidence & limitations

bullets.detail: The source is draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal-00, an individual Internet-Draft dated October 30. It is not an approved IETF standard or evidence of industry-wide implementation.

The draft covers use of an asset to change learned parameters of a generative model. It excludes models used exclusively for non-generative classification, ranking or scoring; the signal is not a universal content-use prohibition.

robots.txt expresses a machine-readable preference. It does not technically prevent retrieval, copying or training by a non-cooperating actor. Compliance depends on consumers and any separate legal or contractual obligations.

sections.title: Key takeaways

bullets.lead: Access and use are different axes
bullets.detail: A crawler can be allowed to retrieve content while its operator is asked not to train a generative model on that content. Combining these into one allow-or-block decision loses information.

Reusing robots.txt groups and longest-path matching lets new policy-aware consumers read the signal without changing legacy crawlers. A shared vocabulary is useful only when consumers agree to honor it.
